title: This Is How I Teach Students to Take Notes for Learning
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. walks through the sequence he uses to teach note-taking as a learning skill rather than a compliance task. He starts by having students take notes cold, with no instruction, so the resulting overwhelm ("I cried") establishes a shared baseline and a clear goal: a 45-minute nightly cap on homework for his class. From there he models note-taking with students almost daily using a document camera, narrating his thinking aloud, and teaches conventions (titles, source boxes) framed as favors to one's future self rather than rule-following. He reorients students toward the real reader of their notes -- themselves -- and toward the real purpose of notes: not rereading (which breeds false "familiarity") but self-quizzing, via techniques like covering notes and giving a mini-lecture to an imagined audience. A "30-minute challenge" forces students to practice being strategic and picky about what they record, and a colleague's "reduce-it-down" technique for condensing a semester's notes toward exam day is added as a later extension. Stuart closes by arguing that teaching a demanding academic skill well is also a way of teaching students about life -- managing constraints, working within limits, and trusting a process.
points: Letting students take notes with zero instruction on day one deliberately creates a shared, felt baseline of overwhelm that makes the subsequent teaching land as relief rather than another rule.
Reorienting students to ask "who is the reader of my notes?" shifts note-taking from performance-for-the-teacher to a tool built for their own future recall, changing what counts as "good enough."

The core insight that rereading breeds false "familiarity" rather than knowing pushes students toward self-quizzing techniques (covering notes and mini-lecturing an imagined audience) as the real use of notes.

The 30-minute homework cap forces strategic triage rather than exhaustive transcription, and explicitly permits students to stop mid-reading without penalty, which Stuart uses to teach that learning is an iterative process, not a one-shot comprehension test.
quotes: The next morning, I woke up to more than a handful of emails from students saying that they had been in tears doing the notes. It was super overwhelming, it took them 2+ hours, etc.

Unless you are obsessively in love with this class material, I want all of you to have a 45-minute MAX time allotment for this class each night. Our job in the next few weeks will be figuring out how to get there.
Modeling is one of the great secrets of teaching. It makes the abstract concrete.

By default, most of them unconsciously assume that when a teacher assigns note-taking, that means that they are taking notes for the teacher. But asking them this question helps them to unearth the obvious answer: "I'm taking these for me.

Rereading produces a dreaded relationship with content: familiarity. Familiarity is that cursed feeling you get during a test where you say, "Oh shoot — I know this!!! Why can't I think of it right now? I'm blanking out!" Familiarity is not the same thing as knowing.

The worst thing that can happen tonight is you don't get all the way done with the reading when the timer goes off. That's fine. Shut the book, shut your spiral notebook, and go do something else. We'll unpack it all tomorrow.
I really do believe that teaching students toward academic mastery is the perfect context within which to teach them about life.
